Shopify Discussion troubleshooting AI-generated summary Shopify merchants are looking for replacements as Stocky is being phased out, especially for inventory tracking, purchase order (PO) creation, receiving orders, and reorder suggestions. The main complaint is that Shopify’s native PO workflow is much slower and lacks key Stocky-style functionality. A recurring theme is that Stocky combined several workflows in one lightweight tool, while most alternatives specialize in only part of the process: forecasting/reorder planning, PO creation, receiving, stock counts, labeling, transfers, or warehouse management. Suggested options include Inventory Planner, FyreTrail, Stock&Buy, Stockroom, Replenly, Restock, Binly, Stock Transfer Pro, and others, with several app developers disclosing their involvement. Recent posts emphasize choosing based on the most critical workflow: PO + receiving speed, reorder forecasting, multi-location transfers, labels, or full warehouse operations. Several commenters also warn merchants to preserve Stocky data before shutdown: some supplier and historical cost/receiving details may require API access before Aug. 31, while other exports may remain available temporarily. No single consensus replacement has emerged; the discussion remains ongoing. PegNorman May 5, 2026, 10:16pm 1 Why is there not more talk about Stocky disappearing? We use it exclusively for inventory tracking, creating PO’s and receiving orders. The PO feature in shopify is brutally inadequate. Using it takes more than triple the time to place an order. lumine May 5, 2026, 11:41pm 2 PegNorman, you’re not alone - there’s been a lot of quiet frustration about this. The thing is, Stocky did three distinct jobs: PO creation and receiving, inventory tracking, and reorder suggestions based on sales velocity. Most replacements only cover one or two of those well. For PO creation and receiving specifically, Inventory Planner is the closest match to what Stocky had. It imports your Shopify products, builds POs with supplier costs, and handles the receiving workflow. Cin7 Core covers the same ground but it’s more of a full warehouse system - overkill if you’re running a straightforward Shopify store. If you’re mainly frustrated by the native PO experience (no email template, no cost-to-COGS link, takes forever), Stock&Buy is also worth a look. Smaller footprint than Inventory Planner but covers the basics. What’s your rough order volume and how many suppliers are you working with? That changes the recommendation a bit. Ugurcan May 6, 2026, 12:05am 3 You can replace Stocky with our Stock Control app. In fact would love to hear your feedback on it. Pasilobus Stock Control - Multi-location inventory counting and forecasting. | Shopify App Store DougInOr May 6, 2026, 12:22am 4 There’s quite a bit, but I think people are finding there are solutions out there in App form. I’m going to suggest you take a look at FyreTrail as well. FyreTrail offers you exactly what you’re asking for, but it doesn’t try to clone Stocky like the others. Instead, it offers you a more “natural” handling of these features: Purchase Orders: Provides full and partial deliveries, PDF printing and emailing, label printing for only the products on the PO and for the amount of labels you need. Tracking of purchase orders and Supplier management. Inventory Tracking: Provides stock take capability, inventory adjustments and history with custom reasons and reporting. It also allows for Cycle Counting, Area identification, ABC Analysis and active inventory analysis. On top of that it allows “fill the shelves” ordering which means you have Low Stock and Target Stock levels along with other bonuses like Supplier MOQ, MOV, Case Quantity ordering by supplier. So, you’re saving time that you are worried about losing with the one-button ordering and the stock level setting. All of this can be adjusted and managed by supplier as well. Take a look - would love your feedback. Moeed May 6, 2026, 6:47am 5 Hey @PegNorman Stocky alternative recommendation Shopify Apps Hey @Shopifymerchant01 For a solid, affordable alternative that’s also user-friendly, check out Fabrikator, Inventory Planner, or Forecastly. They’re intuitive, powerful, and a big step up from what Stocky’s become. Best, Moeed Best, Moeed Synplex-dev May 6, 2026, 12:02pm 6 @PegNorman worth clarifying before anyone points you in the wrong direction - which parts of Stocky were you actually relying on day-to-day? The reason I ask: Stocky bundled a few distinct workflows and most replacements only cover one or two of them well. PO creation and sending to suppliers : building the order, PDF, emailing it Receiving and updating stock : scanning or confirming delivery, updating inventory automatically Reorder suggestions : Stocky telling you what to reorder based on sales velocity Inventory tracking / stock counts : physical counts, adjustments, history If it’s mainly the PO and receiving workflow that’s painful, that points to one set of tools. If it’s the reorder logic you relied on most, that’s a different problem with different solutions. kthoppae May 7, 2026, 4:46am 7 What’s interesting is that most of the replacement conversations seem to split into two completely different categories: tools focused on inventory planning / forecasting tools focused on operational workflows like PO creation, receiving, and stock counts Stocky wasn’t perfect at either individually, but it connected both in a lightweight way, which is why replacing it has been harder than expected. A lot of teams seem to be discovering that once forecasting, purchasing, receiving, and inventory tracking get separated again, the operational overhead starts creeping back in through spreadsheets, exports, and reconciliation. Feels like the biggest factor now is identifying which part of the workflow actually mattered most day-to-day. Curious which side has been more important in your operation: the replenishment/planning side, or the receiving + inventory control side? SealSubs-Roan May 8, 2026, 9:43pm 9 Hello @PegNorman Stocky hasn’t really had a clean “drop in replacement” built into Shopify, which is why you’re not seeing a lot of unified discussion. Most merchants relying on it heavily are in the same position as you, using it as a core inventory workflow tool rather than just a light PO system. The closest practical direction right now is separating functions instead of replacing one tool. Inventory forecasting and replenishment is usually handled in dedicated inventory apps, while PO creation and receiving is either kept in Stocky where possible or moved into ERP style tools that sync back into Shopify. Shopify’s native PO flow is intentionally simplified, so for high volume or structured purchasing workflows, merchants typically end up using a dedicated inventory management layer on top rather than relying on Shopify alone. kthoppae May 11, 2026, 6:11pm 11 That “separating functions” point feels like the core tradeoff a lot of merchants are now running into. Specialized tools can absolutely solve individual problems well: forecasting, PO workflows, receiving, inventory counts, supplier management. But once those workflows span multiple systems again, teams often end up rebuilding operational continuity manually through exports, reconciliation, and process coordination. For simpler operations that may be perfectly manageable. The challenge seems to appear in the middle: when teams have outgrown spreadsheets, but still don’t want the complexity of a full ERP rollout just to keep purchasing, receiving, and inventory workflows connected. Feels like that’s the gap a lot of Shopify operators are now trying to navigate. mastroke May 11, 2026, 6:58pm 12 PegNorman: Why is there not more talk about Stocky disappearing? We use it exclusively for inventory tracking, creating PO’s and receiving orders. The PO feature in shopify is brutally inadequate. Using it takes more than triple the time to place an order. @PegNorman Let’s try this. Mainly PO creation and receiving? Inventory Planner is where most merchants end up after leaving Stocky. It plugs straight into Shopify, stays in sync automatically, and handles replenishment based on real sales data — not guesswork. Want something more modern with AI forecasting built in? Fabrikatör is worth a serious look. SKU-level demand forecasting, one-click PO automation, multi-warehouse transfers, and it plays nicely with Klaviyo, QuickBooks and Xero if you’re already on those. Selling across Amazon, eBay or Etsy as well? That’s where Stocky always fell short and most basic replacements still do. Sumtracker handles proper multi-channel sync and is built for exactly that situation. Just need something simple for PO basics without all the complexity? Stock&Buy or FyreTrail keep it straightforward — no bloat, just the essentials. One thing a lot of people miss — you can’t directly export supplier data from Stocky, so go in now and manually save your supplier details before August. Don’t leave that until the last minute. kthoppae May 12, 2026, 4:48am 13 This is actually a really good breakdown because it shows how the market is naturally splitting by operational priority. Some teams mainly need: • forecasting and replenishment • multi-channel inventory sync • lightweight PO workflows • receiving + stock control • or broader operational coordination And there are now solid tools emerging for each of those categories individually. What still seems difficult for a lot of operators is deciding where they want the “system of continuity” to live once those workflows start spanning multiple tools and channels. Especially once: Shopify, Amazon, POS, accounting, forecasting, receiving, and supplier workflows all start interacting together. Feels like that’s why so many merchants are spending time right now not just evaluating features, but rethinking where their operational source of truth should actually sit long-term. BrianL43 May 12, 2026, 5:38pm 14 There is another thread on this topic already. https://community.shopify.com/t/replacement-to-stocky/587141/58 We found that FyreTrail fits our needs. Many shops are moving to this app as the developer has integrated most of the requested features needed to replace Stocky, plus some that were not included in Stocky. Shopify is not at all interested offering a replacement. The moment Shopify became publicly traded (and therefore owned by an investment firm), they ceased to care about the needs of their customers. Maintaining Stocky was a line item on a spreadsheet they could delete to increase shareholder value. julien32 June 9, 2026, 8:57pm 16 Like many Shopify merchants, we faced the disappearance of Stocky and the lack of simple alternatives for managing inventory transfers efficiently. That’s exactly why we created Stock Transfer Pro. I prefer to be transparent: I’m part of the team that develops the app. The goal wasn’t to build a complex tool or an expensive ERP system, but rather a practical solution that is easy to use, quick to set up, and fully integrated with Shopify for managing inventory movements across multiple locations. With Stock Transfer Pro, you can: Create and track inventory transfers easily Manage incoming shipments and validate received quantities Oversee multi-location inventory directly from Shopify Centralize your operations without leaving your Shopify admin Many merchants today are looking for a simple alternative between Shopify’s limited inventory transfer capabilities and ERP solutions that are often costly and difficult to implement. If you’re looking for a dedicated inventory transfer solution, you can learn more about Stock Transfer Pro here: apps.shopify.com Stock transfert pro - Multi-site transfers: smart drafts and POS receive. |... Move stock between locations with smart drafts, partial receive, and POS-friendly workflows. Built for multi-store inventory teams. I’d also be interested to know which Stocky feature you miss the most today. Your feedback helps us continue improving the app in the right direction. Clement_Foltzer June 23, 2026, 6:38pm 19 Late to this, but +1 on the bigger point earlier in the thread — the gap isn’t one feature, it’s the whole PO + receiving + inventory loop Stocky did. For the full stack, the inventory/transfer apps already named here cover more ground than I do. Where I can actually help is the narrow slice: printing labels for what you receive. I build LabelCraft (the label half only) — you paste or upload your received SKU+qty list, it matches to your products and prints the batch, and it generates a valid GS1/EAN-13 on the spot for anything missing a barcode. There’s a check-digit audit that flags invalid or duplicate codes before you print, and the exact-size preview means Dymo/Zebra/Brother rolls and Avery sheets line up the first time (±0.1mm). Reading from native Shopify Transfers directly is coming, not live yet. If your real pain is the PO/inventory side, the others fit better — happy to just answer label questions either way. kthoppae June 24, 2026, 3:51pm 20 That distinction is helpful. What’s been interesting across a lot of these discussions is that people seem to be finding solid solutions for individual parts of the workflow, but the challenge is figuring out where the handoffs happen between them. Planning leads to a PO. The PO leads to receiving. Receiving leads to labeling and put-away. Then inventory and reporting need to stay aligned afterward. A label workflow by itself is relatively easy to solve. A transfer workflow by itself is relatively easy to solve. The harder question seems to be how many separate systems a team is comfortable managing before operational overhead starts creeping back in. Appreciate you being transparent about where your tool fits in the process. DougInOr June 24, 2026, 4:57pm 21 I get a completely different view. I think people know what they want and have had a tool that has provided it to them (Stocky). I’ve not seen discussions regarding your interpretation about a feature handoff gap. The “proposed” solution to use Shopify native POs is where the handoff problem is at - not current features. Native POs (currently) do not meet the needs of stores and a better solution is needed. Most stores need Shopify to meet their needs in the Purchase Order space. They want POs to support a great many things that only apps like FyreTrail and a few others provide - but it would be much nicer to not have to pay for the services that Stocky used to provide for free. The key to the transition Shopify is forcing is that removing Stocky is like removing a whole set of features that stores depend on and expecting them to just be OK with it. The suggested replacement is severely lacking at the moment so it’s really a slap in the face to those stores who depend on those features. The problem is not a lack of an app that meets these needs - the problem is how a full feature set is being handled by Shopify. Clement_Foltzer June 24, 2026, 4:57pm 22 That’s exactly the right way to frame it — the individual pieces aren’t the hard part, the seams between them are. And you’ve put your finger on the real constraint: it’s not “can we solve labeling” or “can we solve receiving,” it’s how many separate systems a team will babysit before the overhead you removed quietly creeps back in. That’s the lens I try to keep LabelCraft honest against. Nobody should adopt a system just to print labels — so it deliberately doesn’t plan, manage POs, or write inventory levels back. It’s just the labeling seam between receiving and put-away: hand it the received list (paste, a supplier CSV, or — just rolling this out — a Shopify Transfer read directly), it matches to your live variants, prints exact-size labels, generates a valid EAN-13 for anything missing one, and flags unmatched SKUs before it prints rather than after. No re-keying, no separate source of truth — your forecasting tool still owns the numbers. If you ever want to pressure-test that, try it on one real received transfer on the free tier (200 labels/month) — genuinely curious whether it removes a handoff or just moves it. Clement_Foltzer June 24, 2026, 5:28pm 23 Yeah, I think you’re right, and it’s a fair correction to how I framed it. The wound isn’t “no app exists.” It’s that Shopify is pulling a feature set stores built their workflows around for years and pointing them at native POs that aren’t close to ready. That’s the real gap, and no third-party app (mine included) makes that fair or makes it Shopify’s problem to fix. PO depth is its own hard category; FyreTrail and a few others live there, but you’re right that paying for what used to be free stings regardless. For the record, I only work on the labeling slice of what Stocky did, so I won’t pretend it touches the PO side. That part is Shopify’s to own. thepineapplepost June 25, 2026, 11:32am 24 Stock Savvy is amazing! It’s also not expensive! I believe they are doing away with stocky so we have to purchase an app which generates more revenue for Shopify Denis7 July 4, 2026, 2:42pm 25 The tricky part with Stocky going away is that it bundled four separate jobs — PO creation, receiving, reorder suggestions, and inventory tracking — and most single apps only nail one or two. So it’s worth deciding which of those is your real bottleneck before picking a replacement. If PO creation + receiving is the core for you, the workflow-heavy tools cover that. If it’s the reorder suggestions you’ll miss most, that’s a forecasting job: reorder point = (avg daily sales × lead time) + safety stock, which a lightweight tool can do without the full PO suite. What I’ve learned: most alternatives (Inventory Planner, Fabrikator, Prediko) are built for D2C/online brands and priced accordingly ($49-120+/mo). If you’re retail POS, check whether the app handles receiving with cost adjustments and supplier lead times before committing, that’s where most of them fall short. Also: export your supplier data from Stocky manually (screenshots if needed), there’s no export button for it. julien32 July 7, 2026, 8:01am 27 Hello, My app addresses these four issues. apps.shopify.com Stock transfer pro - Multi-site transfers: smart drafts and POS receive. |... Move stock between locations with smart drafts, partial receive, and POS-friendly workflows. Built for multi-store inventory teams. Have a great day MyWorks July 10, 2026, 8:20pm 28 @PegNorman Definitely feel the pain with trying to fill Stocky’s gap with something you can use long term; does more than what’s currently possible in Shopify; and not adding another monthly charge. With Stocky going away, and our own users asking us for a robust way to handle POs and light inventory management / reordering with Shopify; we decided to build our own solution, but for free. Check it out at Stockroom - Stockroom ‑ Purchase Orders - Unlimited purchase orders, receiving & sync with QuickBooks | Shopify App Store - we’re making it completely free for everyone! We think Shopify merchants deserve a robust, stable and long term way to handle Purchase Orders (and the re-ordering/receiving processes that come with them) in a way that fits their business, and not at an additional cost. We’d love to hear any feedback as we continue to build more features to make this a helpful home for Shopify store merchants coming from Stocky! Denyslg August 18, 2026, 2:35pm 31 On ben’s pricing point, since nobody picked it up: the $49-120 tools are priced for D2C brands, where inventory software is a growth expense. POS retail margins don’t absorb that. Which is exactly why Stocky at free-with-POS worked for so long, and why the shutdown stings more for shops than for online brands. The budget picture as it stands this week: native handles PO basics free but stops short on receiving (no labels, no cost adjustments on partials). A few of the smaller post-Stocky apps sit in the $12-19 range precisely because they skipped the D2C machinery - forecasting engines, Amazon sync - that pushes prices into three figures. Mine is one of them ([Binly]( Binly ‑ Stocktake & Reorder - Stocky replacement: phone stocktakes, POs & smart reorder | Shopify App Store ), $19, and it stays there because it’s one person building it and POs, receiving, labels and stocktakes don’t need a bigger bill). Others in the thread have named theirs, and honestly at this price tier the differences are workflow taste more than capability. The deadline detail that matters more than which app you pick: Stocky’s API dies Aug 31, the CSV export keeps working roughly 90 days longer, and supplier records only come out through the API path. If you might ever want your supplier list, get it out before the 31st. Even into a spreadsheet. irish.chen August 20, 2026, 1:55am 32 Before picking a replacement app, worth separating two problems that keep getting conflated in these threads: the data preservation problem and the ongoing tool problem. Data preservation — what you can take with you, and what the deadline actually is: PO headers, line quantities, current cost per product: in the CSV export, survives into Shopify’s 90-day read-only window after Aug 31. supplier_cost_price per PO line (what you actually paid per delivery, historically): API only, closes Aug 31. This is the field that tells you whether a supplier’s price has drifted 12–15% over two years. received_at per purchase item (real delivery date, not order date): API only, closes Aug 31. What your actual lead times are built from — if your new tool uses this to compute reorder timing, it needs real dates, not order-placed dates. Supplier notes (free-text per vendor): not in the API, not in any CSV. Shopify’s migration guide says it outright: “Suppliers can’t be exported from Stocky.” Manual capture only, while you still have Stocky access. Par levels / reorder points: same — no API path, no CSV, internal to Stocky’s logic only. Ongoing tool — the replacement apps mentioned in this thread (Binly, FyreTrail, Stockroom, etc.) mostly cover this well. The right fit depends on whether you need forecasting, API-based imports, or just a lightweight PO workflow. The order that matters: API data rescue this week, then app selection. The app choice is reversible. The cost trail isn’t. (For the API extraction + structured manual capture side, I built InvoRescue — browser-only, one-time fee. Link’s on my profile. Happy to answer what it does or doesn’t cover here first.) Anshul_Sandal August 20, 2026, 7:30am 33 I think the bigger concern is that Stocky wasn’t just an inventory tool for many merchants it was part of the purchasing workflow. We mainly use it for inventory tracking, creating POs, and receiving orders. The native Shopify PO workflow feels much more manual, especially when you are ordering multiple SKU’s. For us, replacing Stocky isn’t simply about finding another inventory app. The real challenge is finding something that makes PO creation + receiving + inventory updates as efficient as stocky did. I’d definitely like to see Shopify improve the native PO experience before Stocky is fully phased out. DougInOr August 20, 2026, 4:34pm 34 @Anshul_Sandal I’d love to get your feedback on FyreTrail then regarding PO Creation + Receiving + Inventory Updates and how it might hit the spot or miss it. I’m very confident (maybe too confident) that your “finding something” that makes that efficient will actually be better (and more suited) than Stocky was. And, if you have relevant and helpful feedback that other stores that have not then you can bet I’ll make sure to implement it. Anshul_Sandal August 21, 2026, 1:50pm 35 Thanks @DougInOr I had a look at FyreTrail and the PO → receiving → Shopify inventory workflow is definitely the part I’d want to compare with Stocky. The ability to create/import POs, handle partial receiving and keep inventory synced looks relevant to what I described. I haven’t used it enough yet to give you meaningful feedback, through, so I’ll go through the workflow properly before commenting on what I’d change. One thing I’ll pay particular attention to is how efficient it feels when a PO has a large number of SKUs and the delivered quantities don’t exactly match the original order. That’s where the day to day workflow really matters for us. DougInOr August 21, 2026, 3:16pm 36 Thank you, @Anshul_Sandal . I appreciate any feedback you can provide. If you do create a PO with many SKUs, just know I have a soft limit imposed on how many items you can add to a PO. If that needs to be higher, just let me know and I’ll adjust it for you. vishalkundar August 21, 2026, 5:05pm 37 Hey, I built Replenly specifically around the Stocky workflow: reorder suggestions based on sales velocity → supplier POs → partial receiving → Shopify inventory sync. It already has one-click Stocky CSV import for suppliers, POs, and product relationships. A few things that might matter based on what I’m reading here: it nets inbound stock from open POs into reorder calculations so you don’t double-order, handles partial receiving with quantity adjustments, and does location-scoped stocktakes with variance review before pushing corrections to Shopify. $20/month. I’m a solo founder; if you’re migrating from Stocky before Aug 31, I’ll personally walk you through the import. DM me or install from the Shopify App Store. Disclosure: I built this app. antalbotond August 22, 2026, 6:14am 38 Anshul_Sandal, since your post is about making PO creation, receiving and inventory updates as fast as Stocky was, I’ll describe the actual flow in my app instead of a feature list, and you can judge the click count. Disclosure: it’s my app (Restock), I’m the developer, solo. Ordering: the low stock page already has quantities suggested from your sales, you press one button on a vendor and it becomes a draft PO with those lines filled in. Check it, press send, the supplier gets a PDF by email. That’s the part PegNorman said takes triple the time in native Shopify, and I agree with them, it’s why I didn’t build on top of native POs. Receiving is the part I’d actually point you at, because I did it differently from the other new apps: there’s a tile on the Shopify POS smart grid. The person unpacking boxes opens it at the till, it shows the open POs for that location, they scan cartons with the phone camera or tap plus a few times, press receive, and stock is updated. Nobody walks to the back office computer. Partial deliveries just leave the rest outstanding on the PO. Someone said above that at this price tier the apps differ by workflow taste more than capability, and that’s honest and true, so this is a taste question: mine assumes the person receiving stock is standing in the shop, not sitting at a desk. $29 a month flat, 14 day trial, on the App Store as of last week: apps.shopify.com/restock-10 . Happy to answer anything, including what it doesn’t do (no forecasting, no multichannel, no accounting sync, by choice). Robert_Dainowski August 22, 2026, 4:18pm 39 worth splitting the decision the way someone upthread already framed it - do you need reorder suggestions (forecasting), or just faster PO creation + receiving? those are usually different apps. if it’s the speed/receiving side that’s killing you, i build stockyard, 15/mo, PO + receiving, no forecasting - won’t fix it if forecasting is actually your bottleneck. kingstore August 22, 2026, 8:47pm 40 Yeah, there are lots of good solutions in this thread. A lot of them are really PO / reorder / receiving tools, which matches what Peg is asking for on the purchase-order side. Useful filter before you pick one: are you mostly replacing Stocky’s PO + receiving workflow, or do you also need bin locations and pick/pack on a warehouse floor? If it’s POs + receiving + stocktakes, the dedicated PO apps here are the right hunt. If stock lives in labeled bins and people walk the floor, you’re in WMS territory. Different job than another sheet next to ShipStation. I work on SKUSavvy which is a mobile WMS, 3D bin map, pick routing, directed put-away, forecasting, and two-way Shopify sync. Happy to answer ops questions either way to any merchant dealing with this upcoming change. tommc87 August 31, 2026, 3:58pm 41 3 Shopify apps, $2.99/mo each — see them all running on a live demo store with real order data Built three focused apps this year, each fixing one specific gap I kept hitting as a merchant. All three are live on the App Store now, $2.99/mo each: Stockler — Flags restock urgency by actual sales velocity, not just raw stock count. Instead of scrolling a spreadsheet guessing which SKUs are about to run out, you get a clear Restock Urgent / Trending Up / Slow Mover view at a glance. Sheafly — Fixes bundle overselling once you’re running more than one location. Shopify’s native bundles don’t account for per-location stock, so you can sell a bundle you can’t actually fulfill from that warehouse — Sheafly stops that before it happens. Trace — Shows you exactly which AI platforms (ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot) are sending you paying customers, down to the order and revenue. GA4 can’t see this traffic at all right now — Trace can. Rather than just describe them, I built a full demo store running all three on real order history so you can see them working rather than take my word for it: stocklersuite-demo.myshopify.com (password: access) Poke around, click into the dashboards, see the actual data. If any of these solve a problem you’re dealing with, they’re all a 30-second install. Resat_y September 19, 2026, 8:44pm 43 Depends which half you’re replacing, and it’s worth deciding that before you start trialling things. If it’s purchase orders and receiving, the PO apps people have named in the longer Stocky threads here are the right shortlist. If it’s the part that told you what to reorder and when, that’s a different category and Shopify admin doesn’t cover it — you’re looking for reorder points, days of cover and forecasting rather than alerts. The one thing I’d check before paying for anything in that group: ask whether it removes past stockout days from the sales rate. The main concern is that Stocky supports core workflows such as purchase orders, receiving, stocktakes, supplier data, inventory adjustments, and reporting, while Shopify’s native replacement is described as incomplete or not yet available for key functions like stock counts. Several merchants say the change creates major burdens, including manually recreating supplier and historical data, losing cost-history visibility, and paying for third-party tools to replace features that were previously included. Some report that this decision, combined with other POS changes, has pushed them to trial or move to other POS systems such as Lightspeed. Recent replies focus on practical migration risks and alternatives. Multiple app developers or vendors suggested replacement tools for purchase orders, transfers, inventory visibility, or cost history. A key warning is that Stocky data access has a deadline: after August 31, Stocky becomes read-only for about 90 days, supplier records cannot be exported, and purchase orders must be exported one CSV at a time. The issue remains unresolved, with merchants still asking Shopify for feature parity, migration tooling, and clearer continuity plans. petgrocer February 20, 2026, 8:09pm 1 Open Letter to Shopify Leadership and Board of Directors Subject: Shopify’s decision to remove Stocky is a material retail operations risk — and it requires immediate intervention To Shopify Leadership and the Board of Directors, Shopify has confirmed that Stocky will no longer be available after August 31, 2026 , and that it was delisted from the Shopify App Store on February 2, 2026 , meaning merchants cannot reinstall it. For many retail merchants, this is not a simple product cleanup. It is the removal of core operating infrastructure. Why this decision is operationally dangerous Shopify’s own documentation describes Stocky as an inventory management tool included with Shopify POS Pro , used for: forecasting inventory needs, suggesting what to order, inventory counts, and inventory transfers. Shopify also documents that Stocky supports critical day-to-day workflows such as: purchase orders (create, manage, track, and receive), stocktakes (manual or barcode-based), with adjustments syncing back to Shopify, and Stocky reporting , including low-stock and ordering-related reporting. These are not edge features. They are the mechanics of running a physical retail business. When these workflows are weakened or removed before a proven replacement is ready, the result is immediate: receiving delays count errors purchasing mistakes margin erosion staff inefficiency and avoidable operational disruption Shopify’s migration guidance confirms major gaps Shopify’s migration page explicitly acknowledges several risks and limitations: Stocky data does not automatically migrate into Shopify (including old purchase orders and stocktakes). Merchants must manually export records they want to keep. Suppliers cannot be exported from Stocky. Some Stocky features “might work differently” or “might not yet be available” in Shopify. Stocky APIs stop working on August 31, 2026 , requiring third-party integration changes. Most concerning: Shopify’s own feature comparison says “Perform inventory stock counts” is “Not available yet – improvements in progress” on the Shopify side. That is a direct admission that feature parity is not complete. Merchant feedback already shows real business impact Shopify Community threads are already documenting what merchants are losing or struggling to replace, including: purchase order creation and receiving, average-cost workflows, barcode-based stock counts, and label printing or basic count workflows without taking on major new software costs. In one thread, a merchant reports support guidance effectively pushing them toward ERP-level replacements costing roughly $350–$1,000+ per month , after previously relying on Stocky for “90% of the lift.” This is not a smooth migration. It is a cost transfer and workflow downgrade. Why shareholders and the board should care Shopify’s own 2025 results make this a governance issue, not just a product issue. In Shopify’s Feb. 11, 2026 earnings release, the company highlighted: 30% full-year revenue growth 29% GMV growth 27% offline revenue growth $1.5B operating income $2.0B free cash flow If Shopify is publicly emphasizing offline and omnichannel momentum, then removing a mission-critical retail operations tool before full replacement is ready creates risk in a segment it is actively relying on for growth. This creates four clear shareholder risks: Retail merchant churn risk POS-heavy merchants are harder to win and expensive to lose. Operational breakage is one of the fastest ways to drive churn. Merchant concerns are already visible in Shopify’s own community. POS Pro revenue and retention risk Stocky functionality is tied to POS Pro retail workflows in Shopify’s documentation (including stocktakes and reports). Weakening those workflows undermines confidence in Shopify’s retail stack. Platform trust erosion Shopify is asking merchants to migrate while simultaneously stating that key records won’t migrate automatically, suppliers can’t be exported, APIs will break, and some features are not yet available. That damages platform trust. Higher support and ecosystem costs Merchants are already being pushed toward workarounds, paid third-party tools, and fragmented workflows. That increases support burden and partner friction rather than simplifying operations. What the board should require immediately This is fixable, but only if Shopify pauses and corrects course. 1) Pause the Stocky sunset until feature parity is real Do not remove Stocky until Shopify can fully support the core retail workflows merchants use every day. 2) Publish a dated feature-parity roadmap Include delivery dates for: purchase orders receiving workflows barcode-based stock counting / stocktakes supplier/vendor continuity reporting parity retail label and receiving workflows 3) Guarantee data continuity Provide a practical migration path for: historical purchase orders stocktakes supplier records reporting continuity Manual CSV exports are not a true operational replacement. 4) Create a POS-heavy retail advisory group Test replacement workflows with real multi-location retailers before deprecating Stocky. I specifically want to be a part of this test so our feedback is directly heard. 5) Report migration impact internally and to investors Track and disclose (where appropriate): POS Pro retention migration success rates support volume related to inventory workflow transitions churn in affected cohorts Final point Shopify has built its reputation on helping merchants operate and scale with confidence. Removing Stocky before a complete, proven replacement exists sends the opposite signal: that retail operational continuity is secondary to internal product simplification. For merchants, that is unacceptable. For shareholders, it is unnecessary risk. This decision should be reconsidered immediately. The honest answer is that “updates cost on receive” means different things in different tools. Some write the invoice unit cost to the product once; some handle partial shipments by averaging across deliveries; some just overwrite with whatever was on the last PO. As you said, the quiet drift from mishandled freight/duty splits doesn’t show up until a margin report looks wrong six months later. One thing worth separating: the migration side of this is actually a different problem from the ongoing cost-at-receiving question. Before you even pick a replacement, there’s a layer of Stocky data that the standard CSV doesn’t carry out: purchase_item.supplier_cost_price gives you the cost you paid on each specific delivery over time — not just the current product cost snapshot. That history only lives in the Stocky API, not in any export file, and the API window closes August 31st. If you’re planning a careful migration (which your question suggests you are), pulling that cost trail via the API before the 31st gives you a proper baseline to compare against whatever your new tool’s cost-at-receiving produces going forward. Without it you’re starting with a blank slate and no way to audit the first few months. On your second question — full export, partial, or re-entered by hand — my own migration pulled the complete PO history including cost trail and received dates through the API. Nothing that only existed in the Stocky UI notes fields survived automated export, because those fields aren’t in the API at all. That piece was manual. I work on SKUSavvy, so take the last column with that in mind. For many stores the right answer is native Shopify plus a small PO app, not a full WMS. What Stocky was doing (and what goes dark after Aug 31) Purchase orders to suppliers (create, send, track) Receiving, including partials, into inventory Reorder suggestions (velocity, min/max style “what to buy”) Stocktakes / barcode counts with a proper count session Cost updates at receive (and for some workflows, average or landed-ish cost) Supplier records (contacts, notes, lead time habits) Labels from what you just received Inventory valuation / stock reports tied to that PO world Shopify has said historical Stocky POs and stocktakes will not auto-migrate, suppliers cannot be exported cleanly from Stocky, and the API goes dark Aug 31. Export what you can now (and copy supplier notes by hand while you still can). What you can do in Shopify without another app Purchase orders: Products → Purchase orders. Create POs and receive into a location. It is not Stocky, but basic create and receive is there. Transfers: Inventory transfers for location to location moves. Stock on hand and reports: Inventory views plus CSV export for year end and audits. Simple “where is it” labels: native Bin name (one bin per variant per location). You can set it via inventory CSV or bulk editor, and bin names can show on pick lists. That is free and worth doing if every SKU has one home shelf. Cost: Shopify keeps a unit cost on the product. Native POs are weaker at rich landed cost (freight, duty, FX split across lines). If that is core to you, plan for an app or a spreadsheet process. Reorder brain: native Shopify will not replace Stocky’s “tell me what to order” suggestions. You can build a PO by searching variants (including by size), but the suggestion engine is gone unless you use a sheet or an app. If your world is mostly “make POs, receive them, count once a year, export inventory,” try native first. Only add a paid app when a specific gap is still painful after a week of real receiving. Where SKUSavvy fits (warehouse floor, not a $0 Stocky clone) SKUSavvy is a mobile WMS for merchants who fulfill from their own warehouse (hybrid dropship plus self-fulfill is fine; pure no-warehouse storefront is a bad fit). Rough map: POs and receiving with barcode check-in on a phone or tablet Directed put-away and a 3D bin map (multi-bin reality, not just one label field) Pick routing, pick-pack-ship, fewer wrong shipments when new hires walk the floor Forecasting / PO automation when you want reorder help again Labels as part of the floor workflow (Autopilot), not a separate spreadsheet export Two-way Shopify sync so admin inventory stays honest It will not feel like “Stocky but free.” Pricing is usage based (roughly $179/mo for the first ~250 orders, then a per-order rate; unlimited seats). If you only need cheap POs and stocktakes, the lighter PO apps in this thread are the better hunt. My business doesn’t distinguish between vendors and suppliers when purchasing so going to Shopify’s native purchase order interface also means creating supplier profiles for all the vendors even though all of my products are already associated with the correct vendors. Has anyone made an app that does EXACTLY what stocky does? I’m desperate for a budget option that can generate POs from specific vendors and utilize filters during generation. Thanks! DougInOr June 10, 2026, 10:27pm 2 Exactly, no. That would flirt with trademark/copyright infringement. However, FyreTrail is likely something you need to look into simply because it handles the Purchase Order flow really well. The key difference between Stocky and FyreTrail is that Stocky (as I see it) handled Shopify’s product catalog for retailers whereas FyreTrail handles retailers and removes the concern about Shopify’s catalog from retailers. FyreTrail approaches the process for retailers who need to order products from their Suppliers. It recognizes a “Vendor” really is a Supplier (who sells the item to you) and a Brand (what sells to a Supplier or you) and doesn’t do the silly things that Stocky does with making you choose a Supplier or a Vendor when creating a PO. On top of that, it also recognizes that your Products shouldn’t have to be recreated 15 times to get them into Shopify. Do it once - on the PO and doesn’t force you to enter the things you don’t need to know to get a product ordered. Worry about that when it gets here and when you’re ready to sell it, not when you want to order it. So, FyreTrail is process oriented… to YOUR process… with a little help along the way. Give it a look then reach out if you have any questions. oscprofessional June 11, 2026, 12:34pm 3 Hi @MurphysBootShop , Apps Similar to Stocky Lokad (formerly known for demand forecasting) PO generation from vendors Inventory-based filters Budget: ~$200-500/month (not cheap) Infoplus (Inventory + PO Management) Vendor-based PO generation Advanced filtering Budget: ~$300+/month TraceLink for Shopify (Enterprise) Supply chain PO management Vendor management Budget: Custom pricing (pricey) SealSubs-Roan June 14, 2026, 5:12am 5 MurphysBootShop: The sundowning of Stocky in August feels like a nightmare right now. My business doesn’t distinguish between vendors and suppliers when purchasing so going to Shopify’s native purchase order interface also means creating supplier profiles for all the vendors even though all of my products are already associated with the correct vendors. Has anyone made an app that does EXACTLY what stocky does? I’m desperate for a budget option that can generate POs from specific vendors and utilize filters during generation. Hey there @MurphysBootShop Several merchants share that the best way around this is to abandon Stocky’s vendor system and use vendor tags or metafields to organize the product information, and then place the orders through a third party system that uses filtering logic. Solutions like Cin7 Core, Sumtracker, or Katana are usually the best alternatives to Stocky’s PO creation and vendor-specific filtering. They provide you the ability to group products dynamically and generate POs without having to recreate supplier records as you must on the Shopify native app. And if you really want to keep it light, using tagged products with bulk export apps like Matrixify (formerly Excelify) can also simulate the basics of a PO workflow. Pipokx June 14, 2026, 8:55am 6 Hey @MurphysBootShop , What type of business do you run and what volumes you process ? Depending on your business specificities, some apps will be better than others, or sometimes, no apps at all are needed as jobs can be done in the background using logic and syncs between your systems. Tell us a bit more about your business and workflow, Thanks MurphysBootShop June 18, 2026, 5:32pm 7 I run a small shoe store which means that frequently I am ordering 2-12 pairs at a time. Currently when using Stocky: I will select a vendor, under “forecast type” I use “target stock level” and set it to 1, apply a filter to only add items with a relevant tag, and then create the PO. Being able to limit my PO’s reach by tags is crucial as my store’s inventory contains dozens of styles and odd sizes I normally have no intention of ordering. kingstore June 19, 2026, 8:43pm 8 I’m certainly biased but the best solution for the Stocky sunset is SKUSavvy. Stocky has a lot of logic based components and SKUSavvy is designed to mimic nearly exactly what stocky does. This includes automated purchase orders with min/max levels, automated allocation of stock across your locations, check-in barcode scanning and printing, complete inventory management with 3D bin mapping and bin-to-bin replenishment, as well as guided pick routing, fulfillment and shipping automation. Additionally, SKUSavvy is perfectly integrated with Shopify providing a dual way sync across all key data types and for all Shopify versions and POS. While this is not a perfect replacement, if you are looking for the de facto replacement for Stocky, this will certainly do it. This is not free, so its hard to complete there, but at $179/month for a full WMS, this is also not break the bank type of system. Give it a try for free or explore the website MurphysBootShop July 8, 2026, 3:00pm 9 Yeah, I’m not even gonna remotely consider a solution that costs more than $100 per month. We pay so much for shopify already, I can’t justify more than $1000 to our yearly operating costs for a piece of functionality that used to be free on this POS and our previous system. kthoppae July 9, 2026, 3:38pm 12 that makes sense. It sounds like the biggest hurdle isn’t learning a new purchasing workflow it’s having to recreate operational relationships that already existed. If your replenishment process already knows which products belong to which vendor, having to manually assign suppliers across the catalog before you can even generate a PO creates a lot of upfront work before you see any benefit. It seems like preserving those supplier relationships during the transition is almost as important as the PO functionality itself. MurphysBootShop July 9, 2026, 3:53pm 13 I agree. But I transitioned to Shopify 3 years ago and I can’t really start over. What do you recommend? kthoppae July 9, 2026, 4:19pm 14 That’s a tough spot, and I probably wouldn’t start over by manually rebuilding everything either. If I were evaluating replacements today, I’d focus less on feature checklists and more on migration effort. A few questions I’d ask are: • Can it preserve or import existing supplier relationships? • Can it generate POs using the workflow I’m already familiar with? • Does it support receiving and inventory updates without adding extra manual work? • How much catalog setup is required before I can create my first PO? If a solution requires weeks of rebuilding master data before it delivers value, that migration cost becomes part of the decision too. Out of curiosity, roughly how many SKUs are you managing today? DougInOr July 9, 2026, 9:23pm 15 I’m going to tack on to @kthoppae 's evaluation, but I really think any valid solution needs to give you an easy way to transition from Stocky. The caveat to you not wanting to spend money on an app for features that used to be free with Pro is that many inexpensive solutions don’t offer an easy transition system. And, if they do, the functionality you need is lacking. I’m not calling any single app out at all (I’m not even thinking of any), but the reality just boils down to how much money an app needs to make simply to be viable. Ok, so it’s a tradeoff… you want an easy transition? Might be hard to find an app that gives you this and gives you the features you NEED for the cost that you’re willing to digest. I’m not trying to get you to come to FyreTrail… I’m really not. I would love to have you, but if FyreTrail is not something you’re even wanting to look at because it costs money then I get it - your priority is then budget and that’s completely fair and understandable. Ultimately it’s totally your choice to either take that risk after the 14 day free trial or recognize it during the trial and take advantage of it afterwards. So what if it’s not FyreTrail? Evaluate, weigh your options, weigh the amount of work you do now and in the future, then decide, “Is this worth my money given what it does for me?” Then choose the app or direction that meets those needs best. You’re first, your store is first, not some app (yes, even my app) that can’t meet those needs. text: Stocky App Going Away after August 31 2026 = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="chat_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-ai_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-events_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-gamification_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-reactions_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="poll_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="9" data-theme-name="header submenus"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="14" data-theme-name="right sidebar blocks"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="7" data-theme-name="shopify"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="40" data-theme-name="custom: set image dimensions"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="19" data-theme-name="header submenus (custom styling rules)"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="31" data-theme-name="hotfix: misc"/> Shopify Community Stocky App Going Away after August 31 2026 Retail & Point of Sale stocky tappacific August 10, 2026, 12:50am 159 Shopify’s migration guide says suppliers can’t be exported and old POs can’t be imported. But Stocky has a read-only API that still works until the 31st, and it gets everything out. Get your key: Stocky → Preferences → API Access. If that section isn’t there, email Shopify Support and ask them to “activate Stocky API access” — takes a day or two, so do it now. Test it works: bash curl -H "Store-Name: yourstore.myshopify.com" \ -H "Authorization: API KEY=your_key" \ "https://stocky.shopifyapps.com/api/v2/suppliers.json" The API KEY= prefix isn’t a typo. Five endpoints available: suppliers , purchase_orders , stock_adjustments , stock_adjustment_items , tax_types . Add ?page=1&limit=250 and walk the pages. Stocktakes and forecast settings aren’t in the API — export those by hand. One thing worth grabbing: the received date on each PO. That’s your real supplier lead time, and it’s the field people don’t miss until they try to plan a reorder without it. If you’d rather not do it by hand, I wrote a script that pulls all five endpoints into CSVs, plus one combined file with every PO line item joined to supplier, cost, and dates. Python, nothing to install, read-only, runs on your machine, no signup: github.com GitHub - tappacific/stocky-export: Export your Stocky suppliers, purchase orders and... Export your Stocky suppliers, purchase orders and cost history to CSV before Shopify shuts it down on 31 August 2026. Read-only, no install. Full disclosure : I’m a developer looking at building a replacement for the reorder/receiving side of Stocky, and wrote this while researching. Script’s free either way. If you used Stocky daily and would give me 15 minutes on how, I’d really appreciate it. Reach me at stocky@tappacific.com Happy to help if anyone gets stuck. Vlad_Gerasimchuk August 10, 2026, 1:44am 160 If you’re replacing Stocky and want reorder points, purchase orders, and receiving in one place, take a look at EZStock. I build it, and I built it for exactly this migration. apps.shopify.com EZstock ‑ Inventory & Orders - Purchase orders, low stock alerts, reorder... Get low stock email alerts, forecast demand, and reorder before you sell out with purchase orders you can import from CSV. Free plan, no credit card required. Two things people are about to lose when Stocky closes on the 31st, and how EZStock handles both: Your history. tappacific is right that the read-only API is the way to get suppliers and old POs out before the 31st. But the plain PO CSV Shopify hands you only creates a new draft on import, so it drops status, received quantities, supplier, and landed cost. EZStock keeps all of it. I made a free browser tool that takes either the Stocky CSVs or the API JSON and converts them into an EZStock-ready file (and a Shopify-ready one), including the supplier_cost_price and received dates the native import throws away. Runs in your browser, nothing uploaded, no signup: Extensions Market Free Stocky Export Converter — Save Your Data Before Aug 31 Turn messy Stocky exports (purchase orders, suppliers, stocktakes) into clean import-ready CSVs. Runs in your browser, free, nothing uploaded. Your reorder workflow. EZStock does supplier tracking, reorder points, low stock alerts, PO creation, and receiving, which is the Stocky feature set most people actually used day to day. It reads live Shopify inventory, so days-of-stock and reorder suggestions stay current. One honest gap for everyone in here: stocktakes and reorder points aren’t in the Stocky API, so you re-enter those wherever you land, EZStock included. Free plan to start with all features fully unlocked for 14 days. Happy to help anyone through the export whether or not you go with it. Custom-Cursor August 10, 2026, 7:31am 161 Hey @carriec228 , I am founder behind the Stockie by Section Kit a Shopify app which helps with inventory. It’s also offers the exporting data from Stocky and import it in the Stocky by Section Kit. This app is currently publicly available on the Shopify app store for use. Aislekit_Support August 11, 2026, 2:39pm 162 Most of this thread is people choosing a PO tool, which is the right first question. Worth flagging a second one that keeps getting folded into it and then surprises people later: printing labels when stock arrives is a separate job, and picking a PO app usually does not answer it. Two things on the platform side that change how you would judge that. Receiving a purchase order in admin now creates an inventory transfer, and the transfer is what apps can actually read. But the transfer does not carry a structured link back to the purchase order it came from. The only PO-ish field on it is a free text reference. So when a tool says it prints “from your purchase order” using native data, what it is really reading is the transfer, and any match back to a PO number depends on whatever your team typed into that free text box. Worth knowing, and worth standardising what goes in there before you rely on it. The other one costs people a whole print run. If you drive labels off a CSV, check which column your scannable values are actually sitting in. Exports quite often put barcode values under a column headed SKU. Plenty of tools decide what to look up from the header rather than from the value, so every row misses, you get a blank sheet, and nothing tells you why. Rename the column, or check that your tool retries the other way round. On the labels themselves, the thing to settle before you buy stock: a barcode for your own back room scanner and a barcode that has to ring up at a retail till are not the same label. The retail one needs real bar height, roughly 18mm for an EAN-13 to hit GS1’s spec, and no 25mm label with five lines of text on it is giving you that. If some products have no barcode at all, a Code 128 of the SKU scans fine in the stockroom and will not work at a till. That is a label stock and printer decision, not a software one, and no app can talk you out of it. Disclosure so it is not a surprise: I build one of the label apps in this space. I am not going to pitch it in a thread about PO tools. The above holds whichever way you go. Denyslg August 11, 2026, 11:09pm 164 I went through this migration with my own catalogs this summer. Your list splits into two buckets. POs, receiving, cost adjustments on receive, stocktakes: several of the replacement apps now handle all four of those reasonably well, and the differences between them come down to workflow taste more than capability. Label printing straight off a PO is the odd one out. Most replacements skip it. If that part is non-negotiable for you, ask about it specifically before committing to anything. Here’s the thing nobody mentions in these threads. Average cost only stays accurate if the receiving flow actually records what you paid per delivery. Some apps just overwrite the catalog cost with the last PO price, which quietly breaks your margins after the first partial delivery, and you won’t notice until a report looks wrong months later. Quietly is the bad part. Run one test order before Aug 31, while you can still compare the numbers against Stocky’s. I’m the developer of Binly ( Binly ‑ Stocktake & Reorder - Stocky replacement: phone stocktakes, POs & smart reorder | Shopify App Store ) - POs, receiving with per-delivery costs, stocktakes with a barcode scanner. No label printing yet, being honest. Happy to answer awkward questions either way. irish.chen August 14, 2026, 1:37am 165 tappacific — the script approach is a useful option for anyone comfortable running Python, and the joined output (PO line + supplier + cost + dates in one file) is the right shape for the data. Good that you flagged getting the API key activated now — the two-day turnaround from Shopify Support is real, and people discovering that on August 30th will have a bad morning. One gap worth naming alongside any API-based route, script or otherwise: the notes fields that live in the Stocky UI but not in the API. The /suppliers endpoint returns contact and address fields — no free-text notes. The PO detail pages in the Stocky UI show notes that simply don’t surface in any API response. So after any API extraction is done, there’s still a manual step if those notes have value: open each supplier page and copy them while Stocky is still live. That’s the part your script can’t automate, and neither can anything else — it’s not a limitation of the tool, it’s just not in the data Stocky exposes programmatically. Worth being explicit in your readme so people know what’s covered and what isn’t. The structured data — POs, costs, received dates — is recoverable. The free-text stuff needs eyes on it before the 31st. irish.chen August 15, 2026, 3:32am 167 Clement’s breakdown of the native flow is accurate — the two-step (PO under Products, then Transfer to receive) is exactly how it works now. Worth knowing you can do that without paying for anything, and the label gap he flagged is real: native admin doesn’t print from a received transfer. One layer underneath the app question that’s worth surfacing with 16 days left on the clock: the API and the export access don’t close on the same date. From Shopify’s own migration page: Stocky APIs stop working on August 31 . Read-only export access runs for at least 90 days after that . That matters because the CSV exports — which the 90 days keeps alive — don’t carry two things that the API does: purchase_item.received_at — actual landed date per delivery, not just the PO creation date. What real lead time per supplier is built from. purchase_item.supplier_cost_price — what you actually paid on that delivery, per supplier. Your cost trail. If those are in the API and not in the CSV, they’re on the short clock, not the long one. The other confirmed gap (no clock helps here): supplier notes. The /suppliers endpoint returns structured contact and address fields. No free-text field. Shopify’s migration guide says it outright: “Suppliers can’t be exported from Stocky.” Manual copy is the only route, and the supplier detail pages are what read-only keeps open — but “export access” and “full UI access” aren’t the same thing, and I wouldn’t assume the detail pages stay up past Aug 31 without testing it. Worth doing: get the API-layer data out this week, while there’s no ambiguity. The app choice is the decision you can revisit in September. (I built InvoRescue for this — API extraction + structured walk-through for the manual-capture fields — link’s on my profile. But the two-clock distinction above holds regardless.) Teddy_Chang August 15, 2026, 3:52pm 170 The separate receiver document is important because the PO records what was expected, while the receiver should record what actually arrived. If 100 units are ordered but arrive in three deliveries, one PO document can’t show the date, quantity, invoice and cost associated with each delivery clearly. Each delivery needs its own receiver ID so staff and bookkeeping can refer to the same event later. Label printing would also be safer from the receiver rather than the original PO. That way labels are generated only for the units that physically arrived, not everything that was ordered. If a receiver is corrected later, the original document should remain available and the correction should be linked to it instead of silently replacing it. maychich August 17, 2026, 12:17am 174 I built a small free thing that might help some of you here. Looking at what Stocky actually exports, a few things quietly don’t come across. Suppliers aren’t in the export at all, Shopify’s own migration doc tells you to recreate them by hand. Par levels and reorder points aren’t in the CSV either. And depending on which report you pull, cost per line can come out blank, which means the cost history is just gone on the 31st. So I made a page that reads your Stocky CSVs, tells you what is actually in them and what is missing, and bundles it into one file you can keep. illustrious-rolypoly-881da4.netlify.app Stocky Rescue — audit and convert your Stocky exports before 31 August Free browser-only tool. Check what your Stocky CSV exports are missing before Shopify deletes Stocky on 31 August 2026, and convert them into clean archives. Nothing is uploaded. It runs entirely in your browser. Nothing gets uploaded anywhere, there is no account, and you can disconnect from wifi after the page loads and it still works. I built it that way on purpose, because it seemed wrong to ask people to hand their cost and supplier data to a stranger two weeks before a deadline. Free, and it will stay free. If it misses a field you care about, say so and I will add it. irish.chen August 18, 2026, 2:04am 175 One thing getting lost in the tool comparisons, and it matters regardless of which app you pick: The migration has two separate problems, and only one of them is solvable with software. What any good tool can handle: supplier_cost_price per delivery, received_at per PO line, structured supplier contacts — all of these are in the Stocky API and any tool that calls it before the 31st can bring them across. Several apps in this thread now cover this well, and the tappacific GitHub script handles it for free if you’re comfortable with Python. What no tool can handle automatically: Supplier notes and par levels. The /suppliers API endpoint has no free-text field — Shopify’s migration doc confirms it outright (“Suppliers can’t be exported from Stocky”). Par levels aren’t in any documented API resource either. The only path for those is opening supplier and PO detail pages by hand while Stocky is still live and copying them out. How much work that is depends on how many suppliers you have. The app decision is worth a few days of consideration. The notes and par levels have 13 days left. Worth treating them as separate problems. (InvoRescue handles both — API extraction for the recoverable fields, and a guided walkthrough for the manual-capture part. One-time fee, runs entirely in-browser. Link’s on my profile.) maychich August 19, 2026, 3:06am 176 irish.chen is right, and my post above was wrong on an important point. Correcting it rather than leaving it sitting there. I was describing the CSV export, not the Stocky API. The API is read-only but it does carry suppliers, and per purchase order line it carries supplier_cost_price and received_at. So the cost trail and the supplier list are recoverable by anything that calls it before the 31st. I said they were gone. They aren’t, and that was the most alarming thing in my post. What does appear to be genuinely unrecoverable: supplier notes, because there is no free text field on the supplier resource, and par levels and reorder points, which aren’t in any documented resource. Those need copying out by hand while Stocky is still up, and there are 13 days left. My page only reads CSV files, so it can only tell you what is in your CSVs. That is a narrower job than I made it sound. If what you care about is cost history and suppliers, use something that talks to the API instead. Sorry for the noise. TinyOpsStudio August 21, 2026, 1:18am 177 With the shutdown this close, I would separate data preservation from replacement selection. The first job has a hard deadline, while the replacement can still be changed after cutover. A practical cutover packet would contain: Untouched, date-stamped exports of completed purchase-order reports, stocktake history, and historical cost data. A manual supplier register for the details the standard exports do not preserve, including contacts, notes, ordering rules, and any par levels the team actually uses. Give each supplier a stable ID in that register. A snapshot of every open or in-transit purchase order showing ordered, received, and remaining quantities, line costs, supplier, and expected arrival date. A reconciliation sheet with source counts for suppliers, purchase orders, PO lines, stocktakes, and adjustments, plus an exception log for anything blank or inaccessible. One representative test in the replacement workflow: create a purchase order, receive it partially, receive the remainder, adjust a cost, and confirm the resulting inventory movement and audit history. A source-to-target mapping table that records the old Stocky identifier, the new system identifier, migration status, and any field that was transformed or dropped. I would keep the raw archive read-only and do any cleanup in copies. The expensive failure here is choosing an app first, then discovering after August 31 that a historical field or manual supplier detail was never captured. irish.chen August 22, 2026, 3:40am 178 TinyOpsStudio’s cutover packet structure is solid — and items 1 and 2 on that list are exactly where the deadline asymmetry bites. Worth being precise: “historical cost data” in item 1 and “supplier contacts, notes, ordering rules, par levels” in item 2 come out through very different paths, and they don’t share the same deadline. Historical cost data — two separate layers: Current cost per product: in the CSV export, available during the 90-day read-only window after Aug 31. purchase_item.supplier_cost_price — what you actually paid per delivery, historically: API-only. This closes August 31, not 90 days later. Same split for dates: the CSV gives you PO creation date. received_at per purchase item (the actual delivery date, which is what real lead-time calculation is built from) is also API-only, also closes August 31. Item 2 — the manual register: Supplier notes (free-text) don’t exist in the Stocky API at all. The /suppliers endpoint returns 18 structured fields — no notes field. Shopify’s own migration guide says it plainly: “Suppliers can’t be exported from Stocky.” Same for par levels. So for those, the “window” isn’t August 31 vs. 90 days — it’s however long the read-only UI keeps the supplier detail pages accessible, which Shopify hasn’t explicitly committed to beyond the export function. So the practical cutover order for items 1 and 2: API extraction this week (cost trail, received dates), then manual register before UI access becomes uncertain. I built InvoRescue, a Chrome extension, specifically for this step — API pull for the fields the CSV misses, then a structured per-supplier walkthrough to capture notes and par levels while Stocky’s UI is still live. One-time fee, runs entirely in the browser. Link’s on my profile — happy to answer what it does or doesn’t cover first. salor_works August 24, 2026, 9:02am 179 Reading through this thread, most of the solutions seem to start with the PO and then improve receiving, costing or labels.
